sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Bot fetches cost the fetcher, so structure saves money
sections.para: Baekdal's week of 16,000 AI answer fetches and 10 referrals is usually read as a tragedy of the commons. A second reading: every fetch costs the provider tokens, and markdown twins cut them by 62% on this site. Every payment rail prices the content, none the format, so a share of the saving could pay publishers.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Publishers can cut wasted tokens and share the saving
sections.para: More than half of legitimate bot fetches re-fetch unchanged pages, and markdown is 62% to 81% fewer tokens than HTML. Markdown twins, dates and hashes, frozen sources and typed graphs remove the waste. A rebate in money or tokens is small per site, tens of dollars a week, but large in aggregate, and only providers can test it.

sections.label: The commons reading, and where it has got to
sections.line: Every new payment rail prices content, not format
sections.para: Cloudflare blocked AI crawlers by default in July 2025 and by 2026 was moving to pay per answer, with bots at 57.4% of HTML traffic. RSL, the IAB protocols, Microsoft's marketplace, Perplexity's Comet Plus and News Corp's $250 million OpenAI deal all price the article or its citation. None prices the form it arrives in.

sections.label: The other side of the ledger
sections.line: Answer engines pay to parse HTML, mostly waste
sections.para: Providers fetch, parse, strip and tokenise HTML full of chrome. Cloudflare's example fell from 16,180 tokens to 3,150 as markdown, 81% fewer; this site's 183 pages fell 62%, from 7,054 tokens to 2,670 on average. Over half of bot fetches are of unchanged pages and over 90% of crawled pages are unique, so caches miss.

sections.label: The arithmetic, honestly
sections.line: The saving is small per site, large in aggregate
sections.para: Baekdal's 16,000 weekly fetches would save about 70 million tokens as markdown, $70 to $350 a week at list prices, and less after extractors, caching and truncation. The argument survives because the site knows what is chrome, only it can signal nothing has changed, and the waste is multiplied across every site the bots read.

sections.label: What "easy to read" means, in four steps
sections.line: Four steps make a site cheap to read
sections.para: A markdown twin with an llms.txt map; a date and a hash so unchanged pages are skipped; frozen, hashed sources that remove verification fetches; and a typed graph that loads only what a question needs. Each exists today, from Cloudflare's Markdown for Agents to Wikimedia's structured JSON, but nobody pays for them.

sections.label: The exchange
sections.line: Providers should rebate publishers for the tokens saved
sections.para: A provider that spends fewer tokens on a structured site should return part of the saving, as a rebate for format rather than a content licence. It already measures the tokens per fetch. Payment could be money over rails like x402, or the provider's own token credits, as News Corp accepted, with terms in robots.txt and headers.

sections.label: Why it might not work
sections.line: The objections are real but none kills the idea
sections.para: The per-site sum is small, a single site cannot invoice, and providers already use extractors, though not for re-fetches. Nobody reads llms.txt because nobody pays for it. The most serious objection is Baekdal's: he wants an audience, not money, and the proposal does not answer that, though structure helps citations reach readers.

sections.label: What this site already does, and what would settle it
sections.line: This site serves structure; provider logs hold the proof
sections.para: Every page here has a markdown twin, releases are stamped with commits, and vault sources are frozen and hashed. What would settle the hypothesis is three numbers per domain from provider logs: HTML tokens, markdown tokens and fetches a change signal would skip. Answer engines take without paying, but also pay to take the hard way.

sections.label: Sources
sections.line: Sources: Baekdal's post, Cloudflare data and payment schemes
sections.para: Thomas Baekdal's LinkedIn post, Cloudflare's crawl-to-click, pay per crawl, Markdown for Agents and AI Index announcements, and the ETH Zurich cache paper. Also TollBit's State of the Bots, Wikimedia's crawler reports, RSL, Microsoft's marketplace, Comet Plus, the News Corp deal and Jeremy Howard's llms.txt.
